```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(rdantic)
library(ellmer)
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
# this is for creating the chat object for the hardcoded chat results
# note this assumes a corporate azure setup with Entra ID keys.
# If you want to replicate it, you can use any chat instance of ellmer!
response <- httr::POST(
  paste0("https://login.microsoftonline.com/", Sys.getenv("AZURE_TENANT_ID"), "/oauth2/token"),
  body = list(
    "grant_type" = "client_credentials",
    "client_id" = Sys.getenv("AZURE_CLIENT_ID"),
    "client_secret" = Sys.getenv("AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET"),
    "resource" = "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/"
  )
)
access_token <- httr::content(response)$access_token
chat <- chat_openai(
  base_url = paste0(Sys.getenv("AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT"), "openai/v1"),
  model = "gpt-5.6-luna",
  credentials = function() list(Authorization = paste("Bearer", access_token))
)
```

This vignette assumes that `chat` is an ellmer chat object that has already been
created and configured. The examples use the same structured extraction task in
two styles: an ellmer type specification, and an rdantic declaration converted
to an ellmer type.

## The same type, side by side

Suppose a model should return a person's name and positive age. With ellmer,
the response type is assembled directly from ellmer's `type_*()` functions:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ellmer_type <- type_object(
  age = type_integer(),
  name = type_string()
)

answer_ellmer <- chat$chat_structured(
  "My name is Bob and I'm 30 years old",
  type = ellmer_type
)
answer_ellmer
#> $age
#> [1] 30
#>
#> $name
#> [1] "Bob"
```

The equivalent rdantic declaration keeps the same shape available as an R type.
`[1]` says that each field is a scalar, and `[. > 0]` adds a validation rule to
`age`:

```{r}
AgeName <- struct(
  .name = "AgeName",
  .description = "A structure representing a person's age and name",
  age = (int[1][. > 0] | NULL),
  name = (chr[1] | NULL)
)
AgeName
```

Convert the declaration at the boundary where ellmer needs its type:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
answer_rdantic <- chat$chat_structured(
  "My name is Bob and I'm 30 years old",
  type = to_ellmer_type(AgeName)
)
answer_rdantic
#> $age
#> [1] 30
#>
#> $name
#> [1] "Bob"
```

If we want to check the answer with rdantic, we can do so with `from_list()`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
checked_answer <- from_list(AgeName, answer_rdantic)
checked_answer
#> <AgeName>
#>   age  : 30L
#>   name : "Bob"
```

This is better illustrated with a text that doesnt conform to the age > 0 requirement.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
answer_invalid <- chat$chat_structured(
  "My name is Alice and I'm -5 years old",
  type = to_ellmer_type(AgeName)
)
answer_invalid
#> $age
#> [1] -5
#>
#> $name
#> [1] "Alice"

from_list(AgeName, answer_invalid)
#> Error: 1 validation problem in AgeName
#>   $age  expected int[1][. > 0] | NULL, got int[1] -5L
```

`to_ellmer_type()` is equivalent to the longer form:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
to_ellmer_type(AgeName)
# is equivalent to
AgeName |>
  rdantic::schema() |>
  rdantic::to_json() |>
  ellmer::type_from_schema()
```

And the `to_ellmer_type()` result is identical to the ellmer type that would be constructed manually using `type_from_schema()`.

```{r}
AgeName <- struct(
  .name = "AgeName",
  .description = "A structure representing a person's age and name",
  age = (int[1][. > 0] | NULL),
  name = (chr[1] | NULL)
)

ellmer_age_name <- ellmer::type_object(
  age = type_integer(),
  name = type_string()
)

all.equal(to_ellmer_type(AgeName), ellmer_age_name)

# note the ellmer type is different, so we need to do some further cosmetic adjustments
# to actually compare the values

from_rdantic <- to_ellmer_type(AgeName)
from_ellmer <- ellmer_age_name

# Both interfaces expose the same response fields and scalar types.
ellmer_properties <- S7::prop(from_ellmer, "properties")
rdantic_schema <- S7::prop(from_rdantic, "json")

all.equal(names(ellmer_properties), names(rdantic_schema$properties))
all.equal(
  vapply(ellmer_properties, function(x) S7::prop(x, "type"), character(1)),
  vapply(rdantic_schema$properties, function(x) {
    if (!is.null(x$type)) x$type[[1]] else x$anyOf[[1]]$type
  }, character(1))
)
```

The adapter also accepts a schema that has already been created:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
age_name_schema <- schema(AgeName)
answer_rdantic <- chat$chat_structured(
  "My name is Bob and I'm 30 years old",
  type = to_ellmer_type(age_name_schema)
)
answer_rdantic
#> $age
#> [1] 30
#>
#> $name
#> [1] "Bob"
```



## Required fields and nullable values

rdantic distinguishes between a field that is required and a field whose value
may be `NULL`. In the declaration above, both fields accept `NULL`, so an
rdantic constructor may omit them. This is useful when validating ordinary R
records, but ellmer's structured response format requires every property name
to appear in the JSON Schema `required` array.

`to_ellmer_type()` adapts the schema for that boundary: `age` and `name` are
both required response properties, while their schemas still allow `null`.
The model should therefore return both keys, using `null` when a value cannot be
provided.

```{r}
rdantic_schema <- schema(AgeName)
rdantic_schema$required

ellmer_schema <- S7::prop(to_ellmer_type(AgeName), "json")
ellmer_schema$required
ellmer_schema$properties$age$type

# JSON arrays are represented as lists after ellmer parses the schema.
rdantic_schema$required <- as.list(names(rdantic_schema$properties))
rdantic_schema$properties$name$type <- as.list(rdantic_schema$properties$name$type)
all.equal(ellmer_schema, rdantic_schema)
```

The original rdantic schema is not modified. The stricter `required` handling
is applied only to the schema passed to ellmer.

## Nested records

The same conversion works for nested structs and arrays of structs. Declare the
inner record once, then use it in the outer declaration:

```{r}
Address <- struct(
  .name = "Address",
  city = chr[1] | NULL,
  country = chr[1] | NULL
)

Person <- struct(
  .name = "Person",
  name = chr[1] | NULL,
  address = Address | NULL,
  previous_addresses = list_of(Address)
)
```

The nested object schemas are normalized as well, including the object inside
`previous_addresses`:

```{r}
converted <- S7::prop(to_ellmer_type(Person), "json")
converted$required
converted$properties$address$anyOf[[1]]$required
converted$properties$previous_addresses$items$required
```

Pass the converted type to ellmer exactly as before:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
answer <- chat$chat_structured(
  "Bob lives in Paris and previously lived in Berlin",
  type = to_ellmer_type(Person)
)

#__TODO__
```

## Validate the response in R

The ellmer response is typed for the model call, but the rdantic declaration
can remain the application's validation boundary. By default,
`chat$chat_structured()` uses `convert = TRUE` and returns an R list. Validate
that list with `from_list()`:

```{r}
answer <- list(
  name = "Bob",
  address = list(city = "Paris", country = "France"),
  previous_addresses = list(list(city = "Berlin", country = "Germany"))
)

person <- from_list(Person, answer)
person$name
person$address$city
```

When `convert = FALSE`, ellmer returns the structured response as JSON text.
That form can be validated with `from_json()` instead:

```{r}
reply <- '{
  "name": "Bob",
  "address": {"city": "Paris", "country": "France"},
  "previous_addresses": [{"city": "Berlin", "country": "Germany"}]
}'

person_from_json <- from_json(Person, reply)
person_from_json$name
```

This gives one declaration for both sides of the integration: `to_ellmer_type()`
produces the response type that ellmer needs, while `from_list()` or
`from_json()` applies rdantic's coercion and validation rules after the response
arrives.
